There is one **hard truth** about success: people less talented than you and less experienced than you have more success than you because they are doing the things you're too lazy to do or don't like to do.

We spend lots of time trying to acquire hard skills: formal studies, courses, techniques... that make you very talented in the subject. But talent alone doesn't go far. Talent is a great copilot, a nice wingman. Nice to have, but not strictly necessary.

What is strictly necessary is working hard on improving your **hard skills**, along with your **soft skills** hand by hand. That will be the key to your success.

Imagine an old Handcar vehicle, those that run on train tracks powered by its passengers moving a lever.

![Loud House series railroad](/assets/images/makeYourselfEmployable/loud-house-series-railroad.gif#postImageSmall)

On one side of the car you have your **hard skills**, and on the other side you rely on your **soft skills.** One does not go well without the other...

![Buster Keaton: The general](/assets/images/makeYourselfEmployable/buster-keaton-the-general.gif#postImageSmall)

I guess you can hack it **only** with talent, formal training and hard skills, but it is going to take longer, and it definitely will be harder. You want to take advantage of both sides of the lever, you want to grow your soft skills.

Think about some elite athlete. The amount of time they spend training the skill, lifting weights at the gym, taking care of diet. Those are the unavoidable hard skills if you want to be an athlete with some sort of success. But then think about the press conferences they have to attend, the commercial commitments with the endorsers, the publicity and marketing involved. That has _nothing to do with the craft_, in theory. But it is an **essential** part of the job. And if you want to be successful, you are going to have to do it.

Same thing with software engineering. Sometimes you will have to look at spreadsheets, answering emails, filling up forms, attend mandatory trainings, write blog posts, give talks in conferences... I like to spend hours in front of the computer writing code, but all those other aspects of the job are **as important** as mastering some programming language or any other technical skill.

I do not necessary love writing posts... it is **really hard** to me, actually. It takes a big amount of stamina and sometimes is a real pain. But here I am writing. Because it makes me a better professional, it makes me more employable. Also, I have the opportunity to connect with very interesting people and establish valuable connections.

You can sum up the idea to the following goal: _I aspire to be the professional with whom everyone wants to work._ That, to me, is the definition of professional success.

# How to make yourself employable

> _Soft skills, are skills applicable to **all professions.** These include critical thinking, problem-solving, public speaking, professional writing, teamwork, digital literacy, leadership, professional attitude, work ethic, career management and intercultural fluency._

These are just a few of many skills that will make a difference when looking for a job. Let's explore a few of them with more detail:

## Critical thinking

Critical thinking is the analysis of available facts, evidence, observations, and arguments to form a judgment. To make it clear, a person with critical thinking does not believe that the earth is flat.

This is a fundamental skill that employers are looking on candidates. Sometimes, engineers have a very analytical way of thinking and a little tendency to take things literally and fail to see the big picture. Because of that, the results are often not what was expected and are not aligned with the business vision.

Stop and think before delivering something that _"does what it is required"._ Does it make sense? Does it add value to the customer?

## Problem solving

Problem-solving is the process of achieving a goal by overcoming obstacles. That is what we do. As engineers, as a company, as a race. Human beings are in the business of solving problems. This is how we thrive.

So, as a fundamental skill regarding the **whole human race**, you should consider spending some time learning how to solve problems.

## Professional writing

Professional writing is any form of written communication produced in a workplace environment that enables employees to communicate effectively among themselves.

This is a fundamental skill that, along with public speaking, makes them almost a super-power. It sounds silly but if you know how to write and how to speak, you are already ahead of the competition. Communication is the most difficult skill to achieve, not only in business environment but in life. How many problems have their root in faulty communication? Most of them can be avoided if everyone had good communication skills.

Learn to write and to speak. It pays off.

## Teamwork

Teamwork is the collaborative effort of a group to achieve a common goal or to complete a task in the most effective and efficient way. Think about a rowing team, all of them coordinating their movements to achieve the maximum speed. That is beautiful team effort, the key being the "collaborative effort".

This is a very difficult skill. There are many instances of teams with the best people in terms of hard skills that don't perform as well as other teams with modest hard skills but a strong teamwork mentality.

## Leadership and work ethic

Leadership is the ability of an individual, group or organisation to _"lead"_, influence or guide other individuals, teams, or entire organisations. Your employer expects you to lead, in any order of magnitude that is appropriate, of course. It doesn't mean that you should lead the whole company to its ultimate goal, or lead a whole team in a cooperative effort... Sometimes is just means to lead a development, meaning taking full responsibility from beginning to end.

You should be responsible of whatever task you are doing, specially when it goes wrong. Everyone is a team player when things go well, where you really show character is when things go wrong. Taking ownership or your mistakes will help you in many ways.

If you choose to take full responsibility of your mistakes at your job, you will gain good reputation. That makes you more employable.

# The money problem

At the end of the day, companies work for profit. When you are working for a company, and you make a mistake, that mistake has a capital cost to the company.

If I, as a developer, make a technical mistake (technical meaning involved with my hard skills: programming and such), this mistake has a cost. If I, on the other hand, make a mistake involving my soft skills (not working well within my team, having poor communication skills, being hard to talk with, failing on my critical thinking, etc...) the cost of that mistake is fairly higher than the other one.

So, which person do you think the companies want? Technical mistakes are cheaper so, in general terms, any company will prefer someone that is **easy to work with**, one hundred percent of the time.

I have seen it over and over again... I have seen geniuses (regarding technical skills), come and go without leaving any significant mark on the company. I have seen, on the other hand, people with less technical skills, thrive and grow inside the company like crazy.

# Take Out

**Make yourself employable:** work on your hard skills and your soft skills with the same care and dedication for both. With those two tools you can choose the path of responsibility and commitment with confidence.

# I want to know more

If you want to dig a little deeper, I recommend this couple of books on the topic:

## How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie

![How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie](/assets/images/makeYourselfEmployable/how-to-Win-Friends-and-Influence-People.png#postImageExtraSmall)

This is a classic. Written in 1936 with lots of valuable insight about how people relate to each other. This book will help you understand the motivation behind different ways of doing. The language may be a little out-dated for the current age, but the useful tips and information can be easily extrapolated to modern times.

## Start with Why: How Great Leaders Inspire Everyone to Take Action  by Simon Sinek

![Start with Why: How Great Leaders Inspire Everyone to Take Action  by Simon Sinek](/assets/images/makeYourselfEmployable/start-with-why.png#postImageExtraSmall)

This is a wonderful book to help you understand how companies work. It provides a lot of examples from real companies focusing on marketing and how the companies present themselves to the world. If you consider your personal brand as a company of one (as you should), this book will help understand how to better communicate what you are, what you do and how to better contribute to society.
